Clinical Vignette: Sarah

Sarah sits in the therapy office with her hands folded tightly in her lap, her shoulders drawn up toward her ears. At thirty-three, she carries herself with the careful precision of someone who has learned to control what little she can. She works as a network engineer for a large telecommunications firm, a job that demands focus and problem-solving—skills she has always possessed in abundance. But lately, even the structured world of data systems and network architecture feels unreliable.

Three years ago, her daughter Maya was six years old when she developed a persistent fever. What began as what Sarah thought was a routine illness escalated rapidly. Within forty-eight hours, Maya was in the pediatric intensive care unit with bacterial meningitis. Sarah remembers the fluorescent lights of the hospital corridor with painful clarity. She remembers the neurologist's words about potential complications, about waiting to see if there would be permanent damage. She remembers the sound of the ventilator and her own body going numb, as though watching someone else's life unfold on a screen.

Maya survived. She recovered fully, and the doctors called it a miracle. But Sarah did not recover in the same way.

Now, three years later, Sarah finds herself unable to sit through a full workday without her chest tightening. Her colleagues have noticed that she's become withdrawn, no longer joining them for lunch. She tells herself it's just stress, just work pressure. But the truth is more complicated. Certain sounds—the beeping of her work phone, the sound of an ambulance passing outside—send her into a state of hypervigilance that can last for hours. Her heart races. Her mind floods with images of Maya in that hospital bed, pale and small beneath the machines.

She has developed an intricate system of checking on Maya, even though her daughter is now nine and perfectly healthy. Sarah texts Maya's father multiple times a day, asking for updates and photos. She has researched meningitis statistics obsessively, which only amplifies her conviction that something terrible is waiting to happen again. When Maya complains of a headache at school, Sarah's mind immediately spirals into worst-case scenarios. She has taken her to the emergency room twice in the past six months for symptoms that resolved on their own.

At work, Sarah has become increasingly isolated. She used to be known for her collaborative approach to solving complex network problems, but now she prefers to work alone, with her office door closed. She finds it difficult to concentrate on projects that require sustained attention, even though these were once her strengths. Her supervisor has gently suggested that she might benefit from some time off, but Sarah resists. Taking time off means being alone with her thoughts, and her thoughts have become a minefield.

She sleeps poorly, often waking at three in the morning with her heart pounding, fragments of nightmares dissolving before she can fully remember them. When she does sleep deeply, she dreams of hospital corridors and alarms. During the day, she feels emotionally distant from those around her, as though she is observing her own life from behind glass. Even moments of joy with Maya feel shadowed by an underlying current of dread, a certainty that this peace is temporary, that the universe has already collected its debt once and will certainly come to collect again.

Sarah has started to wonder if she will ever feel safe again.
